screens.title: Classes, Objects, and Structs in Unreal Engine C++
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll make sense of how C++ classes and structs are used inside Unreal Engine. You will learn to view a class as a blueprint and an object as a concrete instance of that blueprint. More importantly, you'll see why Unreal wraps certain types with macros like UCLASS and USTRUCT so the engine can reflect on them at runtime. Reflection unlocks editor integration, Blueprint access, serialization, and automatic memory management. We'll walk through real code examples: an actor class with UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION, and a lightweight USTRUCT used for game data. You'll also learn the common pitfalls: forgetting GENERATED_BODY, confusing raw C++ pointers with garbage-collected UObjects, and when to use weak references to avoid dangling pointers. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to declare engine-aware types, expose properties to the editor, and reason about object lifetimes. As you proceed, think about a concrete example you might build — a collectible actor with editable properties — and how the engine sees that class versus a plain C++ struct. That perspective will guide the hands-on activity that follows.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Classes, Objects, and Structs
Classes, Objects, and Structs
Engine-aware types let the Editor and Blueprints see your code.
This lesson explains why UCLASS and USTRUCT are required, how GENERATED_BODY ties into reflection, and how garbage collection changes memory thinking for Unreal projects. You'll get concrete code examples and a hands-on workflow for creating an actor with an editable property and a callable function.
In this lesson
Engine-aware types
Why macros matter for Editor and Blueprint integration.
Coming up
Memory & GC
How UObjects are managed differently than raw C++ objects.
Practice
Create an Actor
Add UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION and verify in the Editor.
Visual overview
A simple diagram: Plain C++ types are invisible to the Editor; add UCLASS/USTRUCT and the engine can reflect on fields and functions.
Blueprints
Can call UFUNCTIONs and edit UPROPERTYs.
Reflection
Engine inspects types at runtime with metadata from macros.
GC
Unreal manages UObject lifetimes; raw C++ needs manual care.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These first four objectives ground your mental model and practical skills. First, you will understand classes as blueprints and objects as instances; that mental model helps you design actor types and data containers. Second, you'll learn the practical difference between standard C++ classes and Unreal's UCLASS and USTRUCT: the engine's macros make types visible to the Editor, Blueprints, serialization, and garbage collection. Third, you'll be able to declare and define custom C++ classes suitable for integration with Unreal, including inheriting from AActor and implementing BeginPlay or Tick when appropriate. Fourth, you'll gain a working knowledge of GENERATED_BODY and why forgetting it or UCLASS leads to compile-time or Editor problems. Each objective links concept to practice: you'll both reason about design and write code that the Editor recognizes. Keep a simple example in mind, like a collectible actor with an editable value — that example will appear in the hands-on activity. Think about which objective feels hardest; we'll revisit it with concrete code and editor verification.

screens.title: Classes and Objects: The Blueprint and the Instance
screens.narratorSegment: Object-oriented programming frames your design in terms of blueprints and instances. A class packages member variables and member functions: properties describe the data an entity holds, and methods define its behavior. In the chapter we used FighterJet as a clear example: a FighterJet class defines MaxSpeed, FuelCapacity, and behaviors like FireWeapon. Concrete objects are instances such as a particular F-16 or Su-57 with unique values for those properties. That distinction is practical: shared code lives in the class while state lives in instances. When designing game systems, decide what should belong to the class (shared behavior, static defaults) and what should be instance data (player-specific stats, runtime health). A common misconception is to put everything in one big class; instead, prefer small, focused classes and use structs for grouped data. For example, group position and rotation into an FVector or a custom struct for reuse. This class/object approach simplifies testing and reuse: you can instantiate many objects from the same blueprint without duplicating behavior code. Think about a collectible item: the class defines how it responds to collection, while each spawned collectible has its own CollectibleValue. How will you separate shared behavior from per-instance data in your next actor?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A class is a blueprint defining data and behavior; an object is a concrete instance with its own state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Classes & Objects
What is a class?
A template with member variables and functions that defines behavior and structure.
  • Member variable: stores state for instances, e.g., MaxSpeed.
  • Member function: behavior such as TakeOff or FireWeapon.
  • Instances have unique values but share the class implementation.
Analogy
Think of a class as a vehicle blueprint and each object as one assembled car with its VIN and options.
Concrete example
// FighterJet example class FighterJet { public: float MaxSpeed; float FuelCapacity; void FireWeapon(); }; // Object: an F-16 instance with its own MaxSpeed and FuelCapacity
Common mistake
Putting global state in the class instead of instance fields causes unexpected sharing between objects.
Key Takeaway
Separate shared behavior (class) from per-object data (instance) to make components reusable and safe.

screens.title: Standard C++ Types vs Unreal Engine Types
screens.narratorSegment: Not every C++ type needs to be engine-managed. Plain C++ classes and structs are useful for helper code, pure algorithms, or data local to a subsystem, because they avoid extra reflection overhead. However, when you want the Editor or Blueprints to inspect or modify fields, or when you want automatic serialization and garbage collection, you must use UCLASS or USTRUCT. UCLASS/USTRUCT add metadata that the reflection system reads at runtime. That metadata enables the Details panel to show properties, lets Blueprints call functions, and allows the engine to serialize objects during save/load. A practical guideline: use USTRUCT for lightweight, plain data that needs to be visible in the Editor or Blueprints; use UCLASS derived from UObject or AActor when you need engine features like GC, replication, or world presence. A common misconception is that UCLASS is always heavier; while it adds engine wiring, it also saves you from manual memory work and enables editor tooling. In short, choose plain C++ for internal-only logic, USTRUCT for editable data, and UCLASS for objects that the engine must manage. Standard C++ Types vs Unreal Engine Types means plain c++ is efficient for internal logic; uclass/ustruct are required for editor, blueprint, serialization, and engine-managed lifetimes.. In practical terms, when a plain c++ class is enough and when you need uclass or ustruct. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › C++ vs Unreal
Plain C++
  • Good for internal algorithms and helper classes.
  • No reflection, no automatic GC, invisible to Editor and Blueprints.
  • Lower overhead but less tooling support.
Use when
Logic does not need to be exposed to Editor or Blueprints.
Unreal Types (UCLASS / USTRUCT)
  • Visible to the Editor and Blueprints via reflection.
  • Supports serialization, replication, and garbage collection where applicable.
  • Requires GENERATED_BODY and macro wiring.
Use when
You want an editable property, Blueprint access, or engine-managed lifetime.
Example
FVector is an engine type; a custom algorithm helper may be plain C++.
Misconception
UCLASS always causes heavy runtime cost — the gain in tooling and GC often outweighs the cost for engine-managed objects.
Key Takeaway
Pick the minimal level of engine integration needed to get Editor, Blueprint, and GC benefits.

keyIdea.title: Header pattern
keyIdea.text: UCLASS + GENERATED_BODY + UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION form the minimal pattern for an Editor-visible actor.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › AMyCollectible.h
Key header elements
  • Include the generated header and CoreMinimal.
  • UCLASS above the type tells Unreal this is engine-visible.
  • GENERATED_BODY inside class is required for reflection plumbing.
Pro tip
Use consistent naming: MyClass.h and MyClass.generated.h for predictable UHT processing.
Example header
// MyCollectible.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "MyCollectible.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AMyCollectible : public AActor
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  AMyCollectible();

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Collectible")
  int32 CollectibleValue;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Collectible")
  void OnCollected();
};
Key Takeaway
This header pattern is the minimal recipe to make an actor show editable properties and callable functions in the engine's tools.

screens.title: Defining a USTRUCT for Game Data
screens.narratorSegment: Structs are the lightweight containers you use to group related fields. When you mark a struct with USTRUCT and add BlueprintType, the struct can be used as a variable in Blueprints and its members appear in the Details panel when exposed. Inside the struct you must include GENERATED_BODY so the reflection system can register member properties. Each property you want editable should use UPROPERTY with specifiers like EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite. The chapter's FMyCustomData example shows an ID, Name, and Value with a default constructor that initializes fields for safety. This default constructor ensures newly created instances have sensible defaults when used in the Editor or created at runtime. A common pitfall is forgetting constructors for simple structs, leaving uninitialized members that cause confusing behavior. Use USTRUCT for data passed between systems, serialized to save games, or exposed to designers in Blueprints. Because USTRUCTs do not derive from UObject, they are value types and copy semantics apply — be mindful when you expect reference-like behavior. Defining a USTRUCT for Game Data means use ustruct(blueprinttype) and generated_body with uproperty members to make a safe, editor-friendly data container.. In practical terms, how to write a blueprinttype struct that is editable and serializable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: USTRUCT pattern
keyIdea.text: Use USTRUCT(BlueprintType) and GENERATED_BODY with UPROPERTY members to make a safe, editor-friendly data container.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › USTRUCT Example
Why USTRUCT?
  • Exposes grouped data to Blueprints and Editor.
  • Is value-type; copying semantics apply.
  • Good for serializable, lightweight game data.
Design tip
Use USTRUCT for small, composable data packets like stats or hit info.
Example struct
// MyStruct.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "MyStruct.generated.h"

USTRUCT(BlueprintType)
struct FMyCustomData
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
  int32 ID;

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
  FString Name;

  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Custom Data")
  float Value;

  FMyCustomData()
    : ID(0)
    , Name(TEXT("Default"))
    , Value(0.0f)
  {}
};
Common mistake
Treating a USTRUCT like a UObject reference leads to bugs; remember it copies when assigned.
Key Takeaway
USTRUCTs are ideal for editable, serializable data that designers and Blueprints can use safely.

screens.title: GENERATED_BODY and the Reflection System
screens.narratorSegment: The GENERATED_BODY macro is a small but crucial piece of Unreal's type system. It expands into code the Unreal Header Tool expects, connecting your declaration to the engine's reflection metadata. This metadata is what allows the Editor to list properties, Blueprints to call functions, and the engine to perform serialization, replication, and garbage collection. Without GENERATED_BODY, the build process cannot register your fields and functions with the reflection system, and you will see compilation errors or silent invisibility in the Editor. A common misconception is that GENERATED_BODY is just boilerplate you can ignore; in reality it wires type registration, static helpers, and sometimes default constructors required by the engine. When you see strange behavior like UPROPERTY fields not appearing in the Details panel, checking for missing GENERATED_BODY or a mismatched generated include is one of the first diagnostics. The macros and reflection system are what make C++ types first-class citizens inside Unreal, so learning to read the macro pattern helps understand how your code is exposed to designers and tools. GENERATED_BODY and the Reflection System means generated_body connects your c++ declaration to unreal's reflection metadata so the editor and engine systems can use the type.. In practical terms, why these macros are mandatory for engine-managed types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reflection wiring
keyIdea.text: GENERATED_BODY connects your C++ declaration to Unreal's reflection metadata so the Editor and engine systems can use the type.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › GENERATED_BODY
What GENERATED_BODY does
It injects necessary boilerplate and registration code so the Unreal Header Tool can collect metadata about fields and functions. This is how reflection metadata is produced for the engine to consume.
  • Registers properties and functions with reflection metadata.
  • Provides engine hooks used by serialization and replication.
  • Expands to constructors or helpers required by UObject-derived types.
Diagnostic checklist
• If fields don't appear in the Details panel, check for GENERATED_BODY and the generated header include.
• If compilation errors mention missing reflection helpers, look for mismatched specifiers or missing macros.
Misconception
GENERATED_BODY is not optional; it is the bridge between your C++ and engine metadata.
Key Takeaway
Treat GENERATED_BODY as essential reflection wiring rather than cosmetic boilerplate.

screens.title: UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION: Exposing Code to the Editor
screens.narratorSegment: UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION are the language you use to communicate intent to the engine. UPROPERTY controls how fields appear and behave: specifiers like EditAnywhere, VisibleAnywhere, and BlueprintReadOnly determine if a designer can change a value or if Blueprints can access it. UFUNCTION with BlueprintCallable or BlueprintImplementableEvent exposes behavior to designers and scripters. These specifiers also help with serialization and replication metadata. A concrete example from the chapter is a CollectibleValue property with EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite, so designers can set default values in the Editor and Blueprints can read and write the value at runtime. A misconception is that adding UPROPERTY always makes a field slow or heavy — the specifiers guide usage and many fields are cheap to expose. Practically, choose the narrowest specifier that achieves your goal: use VisibleAnywhere for read-only editor display or EditAnywhere for editable defaults. When in doubt, prefer explicit specifiers and document why a property is exposed. This makes code safer for teams and maintains correct runtime behavior. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › UPROPERTY / UFUNCTION
Common specifiers
  • EditAnywhere — editable in the Editor and at runtime where applicable.
  • BlueprintReadWrite — Blueprints can read and write the value.
  • BlueprintCallable — function can be called from Blueprint graphs.
Design note
Expose only what designers or Blueprints need to change; keep others private to maintain invariants.
Concrete example
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Collectible")
int32 CollectibleValue;

UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Collectible")
void OnCollected();
This combination makes the integer editable in the Editor and accessible from Blueprint scripts, while the function can be invoked by designers in visual logic.
Common mistake
Applying broad specifiers by default can expose internal state and make future refactors risky.
Key Takeaway
Use the narrowest specifier that accomplishes the needed Editor or Blueprint exposure.

screens.title: Unreal Memory Management: UObjects and Garbage Collection
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's memory model changes how you think about object ownership. UObject-derived types and Actors are tracked by the engine's garbage collector, which auto-destroys unreferenced objects. That means you usually do not call delete on UObjects; the engine handles lifecycle. But this convenience comes with responsibility: you must avoid holding raw pointers to objects that might be garbage collected without your knowledge. Use TWeakObjectPtr when you want a non-owning reference that becomes null if the target is destroyed. TSoftObjectPtr can reference assets by path and load them lazily. A common source of bugs is mixing new/delete for plain C++ objects with engine-managed objects — never manually delete a UObject. Also, remember that USTRUCTs are value types and are not tracked by GC, so they behave like plain data and don't require GC. Practical pattern: prefer engine containers and smart pointers for UObject references, and validate pointers before dereferencing. When you test in the Editor, try destroying an Actor and ensure other systems gracefully handle the object becoming null. This mental model helps prevent crashes and memory leaks in gameplay code. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Memory & GC
Engine-managed vs manual
  • UObject-derived types are tracked by Unreal's garbage collector.
  • Do not call delete on UObjects — the engine owns their lifecycle.
  • Plain C++ objects need explicit allocation and deletion.
Pointer patterns
Use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references and TSoftObjectPtr for soft references to assets to avoid dangling pointers.
Scenario
If you store a raw UObject* and another system destroys that object, your pointer can become a dangling pointer and crash when dereferenced. Using a weak pointer avoids that crash because it becomes null when the object is collected.
Common mistake
Mixing manual new/delete with UObjects or failing to clear references before destruction leads to elusive bugs.
Key Takeaway
Treat UObject lifetimes as engine-managed and prefer weak or soft pointers for references that may outlive objects.

screens.title: Create and Test a Simple Actor
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a repeatable workflow to create an engine-aware actor and verify it in the Editor. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hands-on: AMySimpleActor
Step-by-step
  1. Create a new C++ Actor class named AMySimpleActor via the Editor.
  2. Add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) float MyFloatValue to the header.
  3. Add UFUNCTION(PrintMyValue) and implement it to print to screen and log.
  4. Compile, place actor in level, and verify the property in Details panel.
Check
If the property does not appear, check includes, GENERATED_BODY, and successful compilation.
Implementation snippet
// MySimpleActor.cpp
#include "MySimpleActor.h"
#include "Engine/Engine.h"

AMySimpleActor::AMySimpleActor()
{
  PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
  MyFloatValue = 100.0f;
}

void AMySimpleActor::BeginPlay()
{
  Super::BeginPlay();
  PrintMyValue();
}

void AMySimpleActor::PrintMyValue()
{
  if (GEngine)
  {
    GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 5.f, FColor::Green, FString::Printf(TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue));
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("MyFloatValue is: %f"), MyFloatValue);
  }
}
Key Takeaway
This simple cycle — edit header, implement, compile, verify in Editor — is your fast feedback loop for engine-aware C++ development.

screens.title: Avoiding Frequent Errors
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes that cost time during Unreal C++ development, and recognizing them early saves hours. First, missing GENERATED_BODY or the generated header include causes UHT and compiler errors, and it often makes types invisible to the Editor. Second, exposing fields without thought can create fragile code; prefer narrow specifiers like VisibleAnywhere for read-only designer information. Third, manually deleting a UObject or mixing new/delete with engine-managed objects will lead to crashes. Fourth, assuming USTRUCT has reference semantics like UObject is incorrect — structs copy on assignment, so unexpected copies can lead to stale data. Fifth, forgetting to compile before returning to the Editor will produce the illusion that your changes didn't work. For each issue, the remedy is straightforward: check macros and includes for compile errors, choose appropriate UPROPERTY specifiers, use weak/soft pointers for non-owning references, and test copy versus reference behavior for structs. These habits make your code robust and editor-friendly. screens.title: Patterns and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: As you build more engine-aware types, some practical patterns will keep your code maintainable. First, favor small, focused classes and USTRUCTs for composable data. This keeps behavior testable and reusable. Second, document why a property is exposed and pick the narrowest UPROPERTY specifier that accomplishes the goal. Third, initialize struct members with a default constructor so Editor-created instances are predictable. Fourth, avoid raw pointers to UObjects in long-lived containers; prefer TWeakObjectPtr or UObject pointers held by owning UPROPERTY references when appropriate. Fifth, use consistent naming and generated header includes so the Unreal Header Tool can reliably process your files. Finally, create a small test level where you place your actor and verify property edits and function calls during play. These practices reduce friction when collaborating with designers and prevent subtle run-time issues related to object lifetimes and reflection metadata. screens.narratorSegment: Finish with three more essential concepts. First, USTRUCT is the macro for defining a struct the engine can inspect and use in Blueprints; use it for lightweight, serializable data that designers should edit. Third, Garbage Collection is Unreal's automatic system for cleaning up unreferenced UObjects; rely on it for UObject lifecycles but use weak or soft references when objects can be destroyed externally. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll make sense of how C++ classes and structs are used inside Unreal Engine. You will learn to view a class as a blueprint and an object as a concrete instance of that blueprint. More importantly, you'll see why Unreal wraps certain types with macros like UCLASS and USTRUCT so the engine can reflect on them at runtime. Reflection unlocks editor integration, Blueprint access, serialization, and automatic memory management. We'll walk through real code examples: an actor class with UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION, and a lightweight USTRUCT used for game data. You'll also learn the common pitfalls: forgetting GENERATED_BODY, confusing raw C++ pointers with garbage-collected UObjects, and when to use weak references to avoid dangling pointers. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to declare engine-aware types, expose properties to the editor, and reason about object lifetimes. As you proceed, think about a concrete example you might build — a collectible actor with editable properties — and how the engine sees that class versus a plain C++ struct. That perspective will guide the hands-on activity that follows.

These first four objectives ground your mental model and practical skills. First, you will understand classes as blueprints and objects as instances; that mental model helps you design actor types and data containers. Second, you'll learn the practical difference between standard C++ classes and Unreal's UCLASS and USTRUCT: the engine's macros make types visible to the Editor, Blueprints, serialization, and garbage collection. Third, you'll be able to declare and define custom C++ classes suitable for integration with Unreal, including inheriting from AActor and implementing BeginPlay or Tick when appropriate. Fourth, you'll gain a working knowledge of GENERATED_BODY and why forgetting it or UCLASS leads to compile-time or Editor problems. Each objective links concept to practice: you'll both reason about design and write code that the Editor recognizes. Keep a simple example in mind, like a collectible actor with an editable value — that example will appear in the hands-on activity. Think about which objective feels hardest; we'll revisit it with concrete code and editor verification.

These four additional objectives focus on practical code patterns and safety. First, you'll learn to write USTRUCTs for lightweight, serializable data that can be edited and used in Blueprints. Second, you'll learn UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers so you can expose fields and functions with appropriate metadata like EditAnywhere or BlueprintCallable. Third, we cover memory management: distinguishing raw C++ pointers from UObjects and using weak or soft pointers to avoid dangling references. Fourth, you'll practice the hands-on activity: create a simple actor, add a property and function, compile, and test the property in the Editor. Each of these objectives reduces the risk of runtime crashes and increases editor friendliness of your code. As you study, notice how each skill feeds into the next: proper macros enable reflection, reflection enables Editor editing, and editing plus GC changes how you write references.

Object-oriented programming frames your design in terms of blueprints and instances. A class packages member variables and member functions: properties describe the data an entity holds, and methods define its behavior. In the chapter we used FighterJet as a clear example: a FighterJet class defines MaxSpeed, FuelCapacity, and behaviors like FireWeapon. Concrete objects are instances such as a particular F-16 or Su-57 with unique values for those properties. That distinction is practical: shared code lives in the class while state lives in instances. When designing game systems, decide what should belong to the class (shared behavior, static defaults) and what should be instance data (player-specific stats, runtime health). A common misconception is to put everything in one big class; instead, prefer small, focused classes and use structs for grouped data. For example, group position and rotation into an FVector or a custom struct for reuse. This class/object approach simplifies testing and reuse: you can instantiate many objects from the same blueprint without duplicating behavior code. Think about a collectible item: the class defines how it responds to collection, while each spawned collectible has its own CollectibleValue. How will you separate shared behavior from per-instance data in your next actor?

Not every C++ type needs to be engine-managed. Plain C++ classes and structs are useful for helper code, pure algorithms, or data local to a subsystem, because they avoid extra reflection overhead. However, when you want the Editor or Blueprints to inspect or modify fields, or when you want automatic serialization and garbage collection, you must use UCLASS or USTRUCT. UCLASS/USTRUCT add metadata that the reflection system reads at runtime. That metadata enables the Details panel to show properties, lets Blueprints call functions, and allows the engine to serialize objects during save/load. A practical guideline: use USTRUCT for lightweight, plain data that needs to be visible in the Editor or Blueprints; use UCLASS derived from UObject or AActor when you need engine features like GC, replication, or world presence. A common misconception is that UCLASS is always heavier; while it adds engine wiring, it also saves you from manual memory work and enables editor tooling. In short, choose plain C++ for internal-only logic, USTRUCT for editable data, and UCLASS for objects that the engine must manage. Standard C++ Types vs Unreal Engine Types means plain c++ is efficient for internal logic; uclass/ustruct are required for editor, blueprint, serialization, and engine-managed lifetimes.. In practical terms, when a plain c++ class is enough and when you need uclass or ustruct. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a typical actor header so you can see the essential macros and patterns. A recognized Unreal actor starts with includes like CoreMinimal and GameFramework Actor. You must add the generated header include that matches the filename for UHT processing. Above the class declaration, UCLASS tells the build tools to register this type for reflection. Inside the class, GENERATED_BODY expands engine wiring needed for properties, constructors, and metadata. Member properties you want editable in the Details panel require UPROPERTY and specifiers such as EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite. Functions you want callable from Blueprints need UFUNCTION with BlueprintCallable. A concrete example in the chapter shows AMyCollectible with CollectibleValue, BeginPlay override, Tick, and OnCollected. Reading that header, you can predict what appears in the Editor: the CollectibleValue field in the Details panel and OnCollected accessible from Blueprint graphs. A common mistake is to forget the generated include or leave out GENERATED_BODY, which leads to compile errors or an invisible type in the Editor. Keep this pattern as your template for new actor files. Declaring a UCLASS Actor means uclass + generated_body + uproperty/ufunction form the minimal pattern for an editor-visible actor.. In practical terms, examine the header required to make an actor visible to the editor and blueprints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The GENERATED_BODY macro is a small but crucial piece of Unreal's type system. It expands into code the Unreal Header Tool expects, connecting your declaration to the engine's reflection metadata. This metadata is what allows the Editor to list properties, Blueprints to call functions, and the engine to perform serialization, replication, and garbage collection. Without GENERATED_BODY, the build process cannot register your fields and functions with the reflection system, and you will see compilation errors or silent invisibility in the Editor. A common misconception is that GENERATED_BODY is just boilerplate you can ignore; in reality it wires type registration, static helpers, and sometimes default constructors required by the engine. UPROPERTY controls how fields appear and behave: specifiers like EditAnywhere, VisibleAnywhere, and BlueprintReadOnly determine if a designer can change a value or if Blueprints can access it. UFUNCTION with BlueprintCallable or BlueprintImplementableEvent exposes behavior to designers and scripters. These specifiers also help with serialization and replication metadata. Practically, choose the narrowest specifier that achieves your goal: use VisibleAnywhere for read-only editor display or EditAnywhere for editable defaults. When in doubt, prefer explicit specifiers and document why a property is exposed. This makes code safer for teams and maintains correct runtime behavior. Unreal's memory model changes how you think about object ownership. UObject-derived types and Actors are tracked by the engine's garbage collector, which auto-destroys unreferenced objects. That means you usually do not call delete on UObjects; the engine handles lifecycle. But this convenience comes with responsibility: you must avoid holding raw pointers to objects that might be garbage collected without your knowledge. Use TWeakObjectPtr when you want a non-owning reference that becomes null if the target is destroyed. TSoftObjectPtr can reference assets by path and load them lazily. A common source of bugs is mixing new/delete for plain C++ objects with engine-managed objects — never manually delete a UObject. Also, remember that USTRUCTs are value types and are not tracked by GC, so they behave like plain data and don't require GC. Practical pattern: prefer engine containers and smart pointers for UObject references, and validate pointers before dereferencing. When you test in the Editor, try destroying an Actor and ensure other systems gracefully handle the object becoming null. This mental model helps prevent crashes and memory leaks in gameplay code. There are a few recurring mistakes that cost time during Unreal C++ development, and recognizing them early saves hours. First, missing GENERATED_BODY or the generated header include causes UHT and compiler errors, and it often makes types invisible to the Editor. Second, exposing fields without thought can create fragile code; prefer narrow specifiers like VisibleAnywhere for read-only designer information. Third, manually deleting a UObject or mixing new/delete with engine-managed objects will lead to crashes. Fourth, assuming USTRUCT has reference semantics like UObject is incorrect — structs copy on assignment, so unexpected copies can lead to stale data. Fifth, forgetting to compile before returning to the Editor will produce the illusion that your changes didn't work. For each issue, the remedy is straightforward: check macros and includes for compile errors, choose appropriate UPROPERTY specifiers, use weak/soft pointers for non-owning references, and test copy versus reference behavior for structs. These habits make your code robust and editor-friendly. Third, initialize struct members with a default constructor so Editor-created instances are predictable. Fourth, avoid raw pointers to UObjects in long-lived containers; prefer TWeakObjectPtr or UObject pointers held by owning UPROPERTY references when appropriate. Fifth, use consistent naming and generated header includes so the Unreal Header Tool can reliably process your files. Finish with three more essential concepts. First, USTRUCT is the macro for defining a struct the engine can inspect and use in Blueprints; use it for lightweight, serializable data that designers should edit. Second, the Reflection System is how the engine reads UCLASS and USTRUCT metadata at runtime to power the Editor, Blueprint access, and serialization — it is the bridge between C++ and engine tooling. Third, Garbage Collection is Unreal's automatic system for cleaning up unreferenced UObjects; rely on it for UObject lifecycles but use weak or soft references when objects can be destroyed externally.
